prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of laser-cooled atoms, that opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Seven of eight members ranked the optical lattice clock, and all seven proposed the same two names, which is unusual agreement on both merit and attribution. Scientifically it is an instrument-level advance: the magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift problem, so many atoms can be interrogated at once, and fractional uncertainties and stabilities have gone from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18 in two decades. That is experimentally demonstrated, not proposed. Independent clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere agree at that level, with fibre-link comparisons between continents. The measurements have been used for a gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, limits on drifts of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and many-body spin-squeezed clock operation. A redefinition of the second is under discussion. The achievement is concrete, has opened a field, and has enabled other work, which are the criteria I weight most. The two-name attribution is cleaner than almost any other shortlisted entry.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the neighbouring ground has already been honoured: laser cooling (1997), the frequency comb (2005) and ion-trap control and clocks (2012). A sceptic can say lattice clocks are an evolutionary step on those prizes. A second objection is that the headline benefits, redefinition of the second, geodesy and new-physics searches, are still partly prospective, and no new physics has yet been seen with the clocks. Third, single-ion and Al+ clock groups, and the Paris and Boulder strontium groups, have a real claim to credit, and two names compress a large community effort.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first, as I did, valuing the close agreement between theory and experiment, but noted that the committee may want to credit the optical-clock concept more broadly, including single-ion clocks, and that she relies on memory for the magic-wavelength priority history.
responses.response: I agree on the merit and I share her uncertainty on priority, so my 'precise priority' caveat applies to both of us. On breadth, I would resist widening the citation to single-ion clocks. The 2012 prize covered ion control, and a lattice-clock citation that is deliberately about the many-atom, magic-wavelength approach is cleaner and avoids the overlap argument. Where I disagree mildly is that atomic theory is more central than she suggests. The blackbody-shift and magic-wavelength calculations are what make the 1e-18 uncertainty budgets credible, so the committee should read the case as theory and experiment together, not as Ye's engineering alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranked gamma-ray burst afterglows first, valuing an instrument-enabled discovery from a detector builder's viewpoint, while ranking the lattice clock third and deferring on its merit relative to other AMO candidates. He also doubts whether Hall and Hänsch leave room.
responses.response: I take the instrument argument seriously, since I weigh it myself, but it supports the clock at least as well: a lattice clock is an instrument whose figures of merit (uncertainty, stability, comparison agreement) are measured and published, whereas the GRB entry's attribution is the weakest on the list, as he and Eva Olsson both note, with van Paradijs's optical identification and a deceased contributor outside the three names. On Hall and Hänsch, the comb prize rewarded the tool that links optical frequencies to microwave counters. The clock is a different invention that uses that tool. I would not accept an overlap argument that would equally exclude any measurement advance after 2005.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first on the basis that it is the controllable toolbox behind present superconducting processors, noted her own proximity to that community, and ranked the lattice clock fifth while deferring on precision metrology.
responses.response: I ranked circuit QED third and I find the physics case strong: dispersive readout and the coupling bus are real, measured advances. My reservation is timing. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits was awarded one cycle ago, so a second superconducting-circuit prize this soon looks harder to justify than a clock prize in a field with no recent award. I also share her flag on credit: Girvin and Huang co-authored the 2004 proposal, which the three credited names do not cover. If the committee does want a quantum-technology prize, I would regard it as my first alternative rather than as a reason to demote the clock.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as the experimental completion of the electroweak sector, while accepting that the choice of three names among thousands is a compromise, and ranked the lattice clock third.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific importance of the discovery, and I accept that the 2013 prize recognised only the theory. My difficulty is the one he names himself: the credit goes to founding spokespersons, so the citation would honour project leadership, not the decisive analyses, and I cannot assess from the supplied record who made the discovery. The clock entry has no such problem, and its two names are agreed by all seven who ranked it. If the committee is willing to say publicly that the prize honours the detector programmes, I would reconsider, but I would not rank it above the clock on the present attribution evidence.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked active-matter hydrodynamics first for its simple universal mechanism, and ranked the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator entry second, noting that the credit among Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Molenkamp is not unique.
responses.response: The universality argument is attractive, but I note that by his own account the precise Toner-Tu exponents are only partially tested, so the experimental maturity is weaker than for the clock. For the topological insulator entry I agree with his attribution worry and would go further: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe system that Molenkamp measured, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp citation leaves out the theory that the experiment actually tested. I would need a convincing answer on that before ranking B042 above the clock, though it would be my second alternative after circuit QED.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges that the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes leave room for an optical-clock prize, or sees lattice clocks as incremental.

Exact priority and relative weight of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and early demonstration against contemporaneous work by Ye's group and by the Paris and Boulder groups, which I have not verified here.
Whether a third name, such as a clock-comparison or atomic-theory contributor, would be needed for a fair record. The shortlist supports only two credited names.
How much the still-pending redefinition of the second should count for timing.
statement.conflict_note: Two connections to flag. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a scientific descendant of that JILA environment; I have no personal or financial tie to Ye or Katori, but a recusal question could be raised. Separately, my role in the Wallraff-free but Chalmers-led Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology overlaps institutionally with Göran Johansson and with the superconducting-circuit field behind B008, so I should not be the deciding voice on circuit QED. No conflict is apparent for the preferred B037 configuration beyond the Hall connection.
